brief: A shelf unit rated to hold 50 kg of books, with two drawers.

requirements.evidence: A two-storey unit of full and half bases (piece:0,0,0/1, piece:1,-1,0/1, piece:-1,0,0/1). Top covers make a flush shelf about 310×227 mm (deck of cover:0,0,1 and cover:1,-1,1), shown holding a row of books (prop:1). Joints are bolted and edges capped.

requirements.evidence: The configurator only checks fit and collisions. It can't rate load or strength, and the parts are 3D printed in whatever material you choose. Nothing here shows the unit will hold 50 kg.

finish.summary: I built a shelf unit with two drawers, but I can't confirm it will hold 50 kg of books. The unit is two storeys high and three cells wide. Two north-half bases are stacked on the left, each with a drawer on its cut face. Two columns of full bases stand to the right, with covers on top. The two full-base covers sit flush and make one shelf surface about 310 × 227 mm, shown here with a row of books on it. Joints are bolted (lockJoints), and every open edge has a solid cap except two that the drawer frames block. check_build passes, and the parts were checked and don't run into each other. The configurator only checks fit and collisions, not strength, so there's no load rating. It comes to 68 printed parts and about 2.96 kg of filament.

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
